Hey, I just read a great book about physics. I think you’d like it.
It’s called The Physics of the World. It’s written by a scientist named Sylvia Mendez.
Oh, I read that book. It was great.
The writer is a warm and competent guide to the mysteries of physics.
I think it promises enrichment for any reader, from those who know little about science to the career physicist.
And it’s refreshing to see a strong, curious, clever woman adding her voice to the scientific discourse in a field that has been traditionally dominated by men.
I think she is to be commended for making an effort to include anecdotes about little-known female scientists.
You know, they were often victims of “a generation firmly convinced that the woman’s place was in the home.”
I like how the book is clearly written with each chapter brought to life by pieces of fascinating knowledge.
For example, in one chapter she exposes a myth that I’ve heard taught by university physics professors.
I’ve often heard that medieval glass windows are thicker at the bottom because glass “flows” like a fluid.
This, she shows, is not true.
The distortion is actually thanks to a peculiarity of the glassmaker’s process.
Yeah. I like how she cultivates scientific engagement by providing a host of do-it-yourself experiments that bring the same foundational principles of classical physics that govern everything from the solar system to your kitchen table, from using complex laws of physics to test whether a spinning egg is cooked to measuring atmospheric pressure by lifting a piece of cardboard.
Her hands-on examples make her book a truly interactive read.
Yes. I must say this equation-free book is an ideal read for scientists of all stripes, anyone teaching science and even people who dislike physics.

Hi, professor. I was hoping I could have a moment of your time if you’re not too busy.
I’m having some problems getting started on my dissertation, and I was hoping you could give me some advice on how to begin.
Sure. I have quite a few students, though. So can you remind me what your topic is?
The general topic I chose is aesthetics, but that’s as far as I’ve got. I don’t really know where to go from there.
Yeah. That’s much too large a topic.
You really need to narrow it down in order to make it more accessible. Otherwise, you’ll be writing a book.
Exactly. That’s what I wanted to ask you about.
I was hoping it would be possible for me to change topics.
I’m really more interested in nature than beauty.
I’m afraid you have to adhere to the assigned topic.
Still, if you're interested in nature, then that certainly can be worked into your dissertation.
We’ve talked about Hume before in class, right?
Oh, yeah. He’s the philosopher who wrote about where our ideas of beauty come from.
Exactly. I suggest you go to the library and get a copy of his biography.
Start from there, but remember to stick to the parameters of the assignment.
This paper is a large part of your cumulative grade, so make sure to follow the instructions.
If you take a look at his biography, you can get a good idea of how his life experiences manifest themselves in his theories of beauty, specifically the way he looked towards nature as the origin of what we find beautiful.
Great. Thanks for taking the time to answer my questions, professor.
I’ll let you get back to class now.
If there's anything else you need, please come see me in my office anytime.

During the Arctic winter from October to March, the average temperature in the frozen north typically hovers around minus 20 degrees Celsius.
But this year, the Arctic is experiencing much higher temperatures.
On February 20, the temperature in Greenland climbed above freezing or zero degrees Celsius and it stayed there for over 24 hours.
Then on February 24, the temperature on Greenland's northern tip reached six degrees Celsius.
Climate scientists described the phenomenon as “stunning.”
Weather conditions that drive this bizarre temperature surge have visited the Arctic before.
They typically appear about once in a decade.
However, the last such increase in temperature took place two years ago.
This is troubling as climbing Arctic temperatures combined with rapid sea-ice loss are creating a new type of climate feedback loop which could accelerate Arctic warming.
Indeed, sea-ice cover in the Arctic is melting faster than expected.
Without those masses of cooling sea-ice, warm air brought to the Arctic can penetrate further inland than it ever did before.
The air can stay warmer, longer, too.
This drives additional melting.
Overall, Earth is warming at a rapid pace — 2014 through 2017 rank as the hottest years on record — and the Arctic is warming twice as fast as anyplace else on Earth.
This raises unique challenges for Arctic wildlife and indigenous people who depend on Arctic ecosystems to survive.
Previously, climate forecasts predicted that Arctic summer ice would disappear entirely by around 2060.
But based on what scientists are seeing now, the Arctic may be facing summers without ice within 20 years.

A good dose of willpower is often necessary to see any task through, whether it's sticking to a spending plan or finishing a great novel.
And if you want to increase that willpower, a new study suggests you just simply have to believe you have it.
According to the study, what matters most is what we think about our willpower.
If we believe it’s a finite resource, we act that way.
We feel exhausted and need breaks between demanding mental tasks.
However, people who view their willpower as a limitless resource get energized instead.
The researchers used a psychological assessment tool to test the validity of the study.
They asked 1,100 Americans and 1,600 Europeans to grade different statements such as “After a challenging mental activity, my energy is depleted, and I must rest to get it refueled again.” or “I can focus on a mental task for long periods without feeling tired.”
Although there was little difference between men and women overall, Americans were more likely to admit to needing breaks after completing mentally challenging tasks.
European participants, on the other hand, claimed they were able to keep going.
Based on the findings, the researchers suggest that the key to boosting your willpower is to believe that you have an abundant supply of it.
“Your feelings about your willpower affect the way you behave. But these feelings are changeable,” they said.
“Changing your beliefs about the nature of your self-control can have positive effects on character development.
This leads to healthier behaviors and perceptions of other people.”

Here is my baby niece Sarah. Her mom is a doctor and her dad is a lawyer.
By the time Sarah goes to college, the jobs her parents do are going to look dramatically different.
In 2013, researchers at Oxford University did a study on the future of work.
They concluded that almost one in every two jobs has a high risk of being automated by machines.
Machine learning is the technology that's responsible for most of this disruption.
It‘s the most powerful branch of artificial intelligence.
It allows machines to learn from data and copy some of the things that humans can do.
My company, Kaggle, operates on the cutting edge of machine learning.
We bring together hundreds of thousands of experts to solve important problems for industry and academia.
This gives us a unique perspective on what machines can do, what they can’t do and what jobs they might automate or threaten.
Machine learning started making its way into industry in the early’90s.
It started with relatively simple tasks.
It started with things like assessing credit risk from loan applications, sorting the mail by reading handwritten zip codes.
Over the past few years, we have made dramatic breakthroughs.
Machine learning is now capable of far, far more complex tasks.
In 2012, Kaggle challenged its community to build a program that could grade high-school essays.
The winning programs were able to match the grades given by human teachers.
Now, given the right data, machines are going to outperform humans at tasks like this.
A teacher might read 10,000 essays over a 40-year career.
A machine can read millions of essays within minutes.
We have no chance of competing against machines on frequent, high-volume tasks.
But there are things we can do that machines cannot.
Where machines have made very little progress is in tackling novel situations.
Machines can't handle things they haven't seen many times before.
The fundamental limitation of machine learning is that it needs to learn from large volumes of past data.
But humans don’t.
We have the ability to connect seemingly different threads to solve problems we’ve never seen before.

What do we learn about Kaggle company’s winning programs?
What is the fundamental limitation of machine learning?
We’ve talked recently about the importance of sustainable energy.
We’ve also talked about the different theories on how that can be done.
So far, our discussions have all been theoretical.
Now I have a practical question for you all.
Can you run a 140,000-kilogram train on just the steam generated by solar power?
Well, one engineer, Tim Castleman, believes it’s possible.
And his home city of Sacramento, California should see the technology’s first test.
As part of the upgrading of its rail yard, Castleman, who is an inventor and self-proclaimed steam visionary, is campaigning for a new steam train that runs without any fire and could run on an existing ten-kilometre line, drawing tourists and perhaps offering city commuters a green alternative to their cars.
Castleman wants to build an array of solar magnifying mirrors at one end of the line to collect and focus heat onto water-filled tubes.
This would generate steam that could be used to fill tanks on a small steam train without the use of fire.
“Supplying power to trains in this way would offer the shortest distance from well to wheels,” he says, “with the least amount of energy lost.”
According to Harry Valentine, a Canadian engineer who is researching modern steam technology, a special tank measuring 2 by 10 metres could store over 750 kilowatt hours of energy as high-pressure steam, enough to pull a 2-car train for an hour or so.
Energy to drive a steam locomotive can be stored in other materials besides water.
For example, a team at Tohoko University in Japan has studied materials that can store large amounts of heat.
When heated, these materials turned from a solid into a liquid absorbing energy as they change phase.
The liquid is maintained above its melting point until steam is required, at which point the liquid is allowed to turn back into a solid, releasing its stored energy.
Another team at Nagoya University in Japan has tested calcium compound as an energy storage material.
Heating this chemical compound drives off carbon dioxide gas, leaving calcium oxide.
The gas can be stored under pressure in a tank.
To recover the energy, the gas is fed back over the calcium oxide.
“In theory,” says Valentine, “this can create a high enough temperature to generate superheated steam.”

Today’s crisis in care for older people in England has two main causes.
First, people are living longer with a lot more complex needs.
Second, they rely on a system that has long been marked by a poor relation between national health and social care services.
Current services originate in two key measures.
They are the National Health Service and the 1948 National Assistance Act.
This required local governments to provide residential accommodation for older people and supervise care homes run by independent organizations.
They also provided home and community services, including meals, day centres and home helpers and other subsidized services.
The National Health Service was free and wholly publicly provided.
It delivered the best health care for all.
No such vision guided residential and community care though.
The care was substantially provided by voluntary services which worked together with local authorities as they long had with eligibility based on income.
Today, life expectancy has risen from 66 for a male at birth in 1948 to around 80 now.
In addition, there is better overall health and improved medical knowledge in care.
This means an unprecedented number of people are surviving longer in conditions requiring expert support.
Families provide at least as much care as they ever did.
Even so, they can rarely, without subsidized support, address serious personal needs.
Care for older people faced persistent criticism as these trends became apparent.
From the early 1960s, local authorities were required to plan health and welfare services.
The aim was to enable older people to remain in their own homes for as long as possible.
But this increased concern about the lack of coordination between free health and paid-for social care.
Through the 1970s, a number of measures sought to improve matters.
However, at a time of financial crisis, funding diminished and little changed.
In the 1980s, the government cut spending.
Meanwhile, preference for private over public services made management even more difficult.
Simultaneously, the number of sick older people grew.
Governments emphasized the need to improve services.
They did so, though, while doing little to stop the erosion of available aid.
Services were irregular across authorities.
Unless you were prepared to pay, they were increasingly difficult to obtain for any but the most severely disabled.
Why has 60 years of criticism produced so little change?
Discrimination against older people has a long history.
Additionally, those affected by inadequate health and social care are too vulnerable to launch the protests that have addressed other forms of discrimination.

sections.title: Part 1 Writing 写作
sections.passage:
1 Just as the old saying goes, “All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy”, which illustrates the importance and necessity of keeping a balance between work and leisure. 2 However, in today's fast-paced work culture, it’s difficult for most people to successfully maintain a good balance between the two.
1 As for me, some tips can contribute to achieving the balance. 2 First of all, you should develop efficient working habits, because only in this way can you squeeze out some leisure time. 3 It requires you to devote your full attention to the task at hand and complete daily work efficiently. 4 Second, in order to relieve the fatigue and stress, it’s vital to schedule one thing that you are interested in each day and set aside some time for relaxation. 5 Last but not least, for those workaholics, please keep in mind that if you work hard, you shouldn't feel guilty when you spend time on personal leisure, for entertainment is also a part of life.
1 To conclude, work and leisure complement each other, so when you get tired and bored with your daily grind, try to take some time off work to relax yourself.

sections.title: Part 4 Translation
sections.passage: 1 In recent years, more and more museums in China have been open to the public free of charge. 2 The number of museum exhibitions and visitors to museums has seen an obvious increase. 3 It has become very common to see that people stand in long queues in front of some widely popular museums. 4 Therefore, these museums must take measures to restrict the number of visitors. 5 Nowadays, the forms of exhibitions become increasingly diverse. 6 Some large museums use advanced technologies such as multimedia and virtual reality to make their exhibitions more attractive. 7 Quite a few museums also hold online exhibitions where people can enjoy the sight of rare and precious exhibits. 8 However, the experience of viewing the exhibits on site is still more appealing to most visitors.

questions.stem: ①近年来，中国越来越多的博物馆免费向公众开放。②博物馆展览次数和参观人数都明显增长。③在一些广受欢迎的博物馆门前，排长队已很常见。④这些博物馆必须采取措施限制参观人数。⑤如今，展览形式越来越多样。⑥一些大型博物馆利用多媒体和虚拟现实等先进技术，使展览更具吸引力。⑦不少博物馆还举办在线展览，人们可在网上观赏珍稀展品。⑧然而，现场观看展品的体验对大多数参观者还是更具吸引力。
questions.answer: 1 In recent years, more and more museums in China have been open to the public free of charge. 2 The number of museum exhibitions and visitors to museums has seen an obvious increase. 3 It has become very common to see that people stand in long queues in front of some widely popular museums. 4 Therefore, these museums must take measures to restrict the number of visitors. 5 Nowadays, the forms of exhibitions become increasingly diverse. 6 Some large museums use advanced technologies such as multimedia and virtual reality to make their exhibitions more attractive. 7 Quite a few museums also hold online exhibitions where people can enjoy the sight of rare and precious exhibits. 8 However, the experience of viewing the exhibits on site is still more appealing to most visitors.

sections.title: Section A 选词填空
sections.passage:
1 Just off the coast of Southern California sits Santa Cruz Island, where a magical creature called the island fox 1.? 2 A decade ago, this island’s ecosystem was in 2.? 3 Wild pigs attracted golden eagles from the mainland, and those flying 3 crashed the fox population.? 4 So the Nature Conservancy launched a 4 war against the pigs, complete with helicopters and sharp shooters.?
1 And it worked. 2 Today, federal agencies are pulling the island fox from the Endangered Species List. 3 It’s the fastest-ever recovery of a mammal, joining peers like the Louisiana black bear as glowing successes in the history of the Endangered Species Act.
1 But the recovery of Santa Cruz Island isn’t just about the fox. 2 The Nature Conservancy has 5 war on a multitude of invasive species here, from sheep to plants to the 6 Argentine ant.? 3 “ Our philosophy with the island has always been, ‘Ok, 7 the threats and let the island go back to what it was, ’ “ says ecologist Christina Boser.? 4 And it appears to be working. 5 Native plants are coming back, and the fox once again bounds about carefree.
1 But keeping those foxes from harm will occupy Boser and her colleagues for years to come. 2 You see, humans are still allowed on Santa Cruz Island, and they bring dogs. 3 So Boser has to vaccinate her foxes against various diseases. 4 “ We’re obligated to keep a pulse on the population for at least five years after the foxes are delisted, “ says Boser. 5 That includes tagging the foxes and 8 their numbers to ensure nothing goes wrong.?
1 This is the story of the little fox that has come back, and the people who have 9 their lives to protecting it.? 2 This is the story of wildlife conservation in the age of mass 10.?

questions.explanation:
【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于where引导的定语从句中，主语为a magical creature，而 called the island fox作后置定语修饰主语，故空格需填入动词充当从句的谓语。另外，该句为陈述客观事实，所以应使用一般现在时，主语creature为单数，空格需填入谓语动词的第三人称单数形式。

【答案解析】

分析备选动词可知，符合语法要求的只有F）dwells和I）hinders。根据本句句意及下文可知，岛屿灰狐居住在圣克鲁斯岛上，故选F) dwells“居住，栖息”。hinders意为“阻碍，妨碍”，代入句中与句意不符，故排除。

【考点】

名词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于介词in之后，需要填入名词或动名词。

【答案解析】

空格所在句指出，10年之前，这座岛屿的生态系统________。由下文可知，岛上的野猪引来了大陆的金雕，导致岛屿灰狐的数量大下降。由此可推出生态系统遭到了破坏，故应选B）chaos“混乱，紊乱”。in chaos为固定用法，表示“处于混乱状态，陷入混乱”。

【考点】

名词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格前出现了限定词those和形容词flying，故空格需要填入名词复数作句子的主语。

【答案解析】

分析句子结构可知，those flying ________指的就是前面提到的金雕。根据空格所在句可知，圣克鲁斯岛上的野猪引来了金雕，结果造成灰狐的数量减少，故推测金雕对野猪和灰狐都进行了捕食，L）predators“捕食性动物”符合文章意思，故为答案。金雕是鸟类，不属于mammal“哺乳动物”，而且mammal也不符合语法，故排除J）。

【考点】

形容词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于冠词a和名词war之间，故需要填入形容词。

【答案解析】

根据空格所在句可知，这场反对野猪的战争配备了直升机和神枪手，故应填入H）fierce“激烈的”来修饰这场野生生物保护战的程度。aggressive也可以用来修饰 war,但是指“侵略战争”，用在这里程度太过，而且aggressive是元音音素开头，需要an来修饰，故排除。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于助动词has和名词war之间，应填入动词的过去分词。

【答案解析】

由上下文可知，此处的________ war和第一段末句中的 launched a fierce war“发起了一场激烈的战役”意思一致。结合备选项，应填入D）declared“宣布，声明”，构成搭配declare war on...“向……宣战”。

【考点】

形容词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于冠词the和名词Argentine ant之间，需要填入形容词。

【答案解析】

分析句子可知，美国大自然保护协会要扫除众多入侵物种，而阿根廷蚁就是其中一种，故填入A）aggressive“好斗的”，用来形容阿根廷蚁对当地造成的生态危害。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

分析句子可知，空格后的and连接平行结构，and后是动词原形和名词构成的动宾结构，故空格处也应填入动词原形。

【答案解析】

空格所在部分指出，________威胁，让岛屿回归它原本的样子。威胁不在了，岛屿才能回归它原本的样子，故填入M）remove“消除”。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格所在处也是and连接平行结构，and前是动词现在分词和名词构成的动宾结构，故空格处也应填入动词现在分词。

【答案解析】

空格上一句中的keep a pulse on...意为“持续关注……”，空格前的 tagging the foxes意为“给灰狐挂上标牌（以进行追踪）”，由此可知博瑟及其同事要继续关注灰狐数量，因此填入K）monitoring“监控，监测”。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于助动词have和名词词组their lives之间，故应填入动词的过去分词，且该词能和后面的介词to搭配。

【答案解析】

who引导的定语从句用来修饰先行词people,并且出现了protecting“保护”一词，由此可知，这里的people指的就是像博瑟这样为保护灰狐付出努力的人，故填入E）dedicated“致力于，献身于”。dedicate oneself/one's life to sth./doing sth.为固定搭配。

【考点】

名词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于介词of和形容词mass之后，应填人名词。

【答案解析】

最后一段将保护圣克鲁斯岛野生生物的意义升华，空格前面的in the age of表示“在……的时代”。结合全文内容和常识，填入G）extinction“灭绝”，和前面的mass“大规模的”搭配，表示物种大灭绝时代，在这样的时代保护野生生物的意义才更显重大，故选G）。

sections.title: Section B 快速阅读
sections.passage:
1 When Katlyn Burbidge’s son was 6 years old, he was performing some ridiculous song and dance typical of a first-grader. 2 But after she snapped a photo and started using her phone, he asked her a serious question: “Are you going to post that online?” 3 She laughed and answered, “Yes, I think I will.” What he said next stopped her. 4 “Can you not?”?
1 That’s when it dawned on her: She had been posting photos of him online without asking his permission. 2 “We’re big advocates of bodily autonomy and not forcing him to hug or kiss people unless he wants to, but it never occurred to me that I should ask his permission to post photos of him online,” says Burbidge, a mom of two in Wakefield, Massachusetts. 3 “Now when I post a photo of him online, I show him the photo and get his okay.”?
1 When her 8-month-old is 3 or 4 years old, she plans to start asking him in an age-appropriate way, “Do you want other people to see this?” 2 That's precisely the approach that two researchers advocated before a room of pediatricians （儿科医生）last week at the American Academy of Pediatrics meeting, when they discussed the 21st century challenge of “sharenting,” a new term for parents ’ online sharing about their children. 3 “As advocates of children ’s rights, we believe that children should have a voice about what information is shared about them if possible,” says Stacey Steinberg, a legal skills professor at the University of Florida Levin College of Law in Gainesville.
1 Whether it’s ensuring that your child isn’t bullied over something you post, that their identity isn’t digitally “kidnapped”, or that their photos don’t end up on a half dozen child pornography (色情) sites, as one Australian mom discovered, parents and pediatricians are increasingly aware of the importance of protecting children ’s digital presence. 2 Steinberg and Bahareh Keith, an assistant professor of pediatrics at the University of Florida College of Medicine, say most children will likely never experience problems related to what their parents share, but a tension still exists between parents ’ rights to share their experiences and their children ’s rights to privacy.?
1 “We’re in no way trying to silence parents ’ voices,” Steinberg says. 2 “At the same time, we recognize that children might have an interest in entering adulthood free to create their own digital footprint.” 3 They cited a study presented earlier this year of 249 pairs of parents and their children in which twice as many children as parents wanted rules on what parents could share. 4 “The parents said, ‘We don’t need rules — we’re fine,’ and the children said, ‘ Our parents need rules,’” Keith says. 5 “The children wanted autonomy about this issue and were worried about their parents sharing information about them.”?
1 Although the American Academy of Pediatrics offers guidelines recommending that parents model appropriate social media use for their children, it does not explicitly discuss oversharing by parents. 2 “I think this is a very legitimate concern, and I appreciate their drawing our attention to it,” David Hill, a father of five, says. 3 He sees a role for pediatricians to talk with parents about this, but believes the messaging must extend far beyond pediatricians ’ offices. 4 “I look forward to seeing researchers expand our understanding of the issue so we can translate it into effective education and policy,” he says.
1 There’s been little research on the topic, Steinberg wrote in a law article about this issue. 2 While states could pass laws related to sharing information about children online, Steinberg feels parents themselves are generally best suited to make these decisions for their families. 3 “While we didn’t want to create any unnecessary panic, we did find some concerns that were troublesome, and we thought that parents or at least physicians should be aware of those potential risks,” Steinberg says. 4 They include photos repurposed for inappropriate or illegal means, identity theft, embarrassment, bullying by peers or digital kidnapping.?
1 But that’s the negative side, with risks that must be balanced against the benefits of sharing. 2 Steinberg pointed out that parental sharing on social media helps build communities, connect spread-out families, provide support and raise awareness around important social issues for which parents might be their children ’s only voice.?
1 A C.S. Mott survey found among the 56 percent of mothers and 34 percent of fathers who discussed parenting on social media, 72 percent of them said sharing made them feel less alone, and nearly as many said sharing helped them worry less and gave them advice from other parents. 2 The most common topics they discussed included kids ’ sleep, nutrition, discipline, behavior problems and day care and preschool.
1 “There ’s this peer-to-peer nature of health care these days with a profound opportunity for parents to learn helpful tips, safety and prevention efforts, pro-vaccine messages and all kinds of other messages from other parents in their social communities,” says Wendy Sue Swanson, a pediatrician and executive director of digital health at Seattle Children ’s Hospital, where she blogs about her own parenting journey to help other parents. 2 “They’re getting nurtured by people they’ve already selected that they trust,” she says.?
1 “How do we weigh the risks, how do we think about the benefits, and how do we alleviate the risks?” she says. 2 “ Those are the questions we need to ask ourselves, and everyone can have a different answer.”
1 Some parents find the best route for them is not to share at all. 2 Bridget O’Hanlon and her husband, who live in Cleveland, decided before their daughter was born that they would not post her photos online. 3 When a few family members did post pictures, O’Hanlon and her husband made their wishes clear. 4 “It’s been hard not to share pictures of her because people always want to know how babies and toddlers (学走路的孩子) are doing and to see pictures, but we made the decision to have social media while she did not,” O’Hanlon said. 5 Similarly, Alison Jamison of New York decided with her husband that their child had a right to their own online identity. 6 They did use an invitation-only photo sharing platform so that friends and family, including those far away, could see the photos, but they stood firm, simply refusing to put their child ’s photos on other social media platforms.?
1 “ For most families, it’s a journey. 2 Sometimes it goes wrong, but most of the time it doesn't,” says Swanson, who recommends starting to ask children permission to post narratives or photos around ages 6 to 8. 3 “We’ll learn more and more what our tolerance is. 4 We can ask our kids to help us learn as a society what’s okay and what’s not.”?
1 Indeed, that learning process goes both ways. 2 Bria Dunham, a mother in Somerville, Massachusetts, was so excited to watch a moment of brotherly bonding while her first-grader and baby took a bath together that she snapped a few photos. 3 But when she considered posting them online, she took the perspective of her son: How would he feel if his classmates ’ parents saw photos of him chest-up in the bathtub? 4 “It made me think about how I’m teaching him to have ownership of his own body and how what is shared today endures into the future,” Dunham says. 5 “ So I kept the pictures to myself and accepted this as one more step in supporting his increasing autonomy.”?

questions.explanation:
【定位】

由题干中的Steinberg和beneficial定位到H）段。

 

【答案解析】

细节归纳题。定位段第一句提到，风险必须与分享的益处相平衡。随后一句引用斯坦伯格的说法来具体阐述在社交媒体上进行育儿分享的好处。题干是对定位段的归纳和概括，故答案为H）。

【定位】

由题干中的expert、school age、help...learn和what can and cannot be done定位到M）段。

 

【答案解析】

细节辨认题。定位段第二句中who引导的定语从句提到，斯旺森建议从孩子6至8岁左右就开始对是否发布他们的故事或照片征得他们的许可。第三、四句描述了斯旺森的观点：我们会对自己的容忍度越来越了解。我们可以让我们的孩子帮助我们了解在社会上什么能做，什么不能做。由此可知，题干中的school age和help their parents learn what can and cannot be done分别对应定位段中的around ages 6 to 8和help us learn as a society what's okay and what’s not，故答案为M）。

【定位】

由题干中的One mother和from her son’s perspective定位到N）段第二、三句。

 

【答案解析】

细节归纳题。定位句提到，当这位母亲考虑将照片放到网上时，她选择了从儿子的角度来考虑。段末又提到，她把这些照片留给自己看（So I kept the pictures to myself），这说明她克制了在网上发布照片的想法。题干中的from her son’s perspective对应原文中的 she took the perspective of her son，故答案为N）。

【定位】

由题干中的a study和rules定位到E）段第三句。

 

【答案解析】

细节辨认题。定位句提到，研究人员引用了今年早些时候发布的一项针对249对父母及其孩子进行的研究，其中，希望规范父母分享内容的孩子是父母的两倍。题干中的more children than parents和rules on parents’ sharing分别对应定位句中的 twice as many children as parents和rules on what parents could share，故答案为E）。

【定位】

由题干中的Katlyn Burbidge和ask her son’s approval定位到B）段第一句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，就在那时凯特琳·伯比奇恍然大悟：她一直在网上发布儿子的照片而没有征得他的同意。定位句中的She就是Katlyn Burbidge。题干中的realized和 never...ask her son’s approval分别对应定位句中的dawned on和without asking his permission，故答案为B）。

【定位】

由题干中的post her son’s photo online及he asked her not to定位到A）段。

 

【答案解析】

细节归纳题。定位段提到，凯特琳·伯比奇正打算在网上分享孩子的照片时，孩子问她是否要在网上发布，并请求她不要这样做（Can you not?），孩子说的话阻止了这位母亲。题干中的decided not to和 post her son’s photo online分别对应原文中的stopped和post that online,故答案为A）。

【定位】

由题干中的pediatrician、help other parents 和  sharing her own parenting experience定位到J）段。

 

【答案解析】

细节辨认题。定位段提到了西雅图儿童医院的儿科医师兼数字健康协会执行主任温迪·苏·斯旺森的观点，她在医院写博客介绍自己在育儿方面的经历来帮助其他父母。题干中的help other parents by sharing her own parenting experience对应原文中的 blogs about her own parenting journey to help other parents，故答案为J）。

【定位】

由题干中的simply not to share定位到L）段首句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，有些父母认为对于他们而言最好的办法就是完全不分享。题干中的simply not to share 是对定位句中not to share at all的同义转述，故答案为L）。

【定位】

由题干中的Parents and physicians和risks定位到G）段第三句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句中提到，我们认为父母或至少是医生应该意识到这些潜在的风险。题干中的Parents and physicians对应定位句中的parents or at least physicians，题干中的realize对应定位句中的be aware of，故答案为G）。

【定位】

由题干中的parenting experiences和children’s privacy定位到D）段最后一句。

 

【答案解析】

细节辨认题。定位句中提到，父母分享孩子经历的权利与孩子们的隐私权之间仍然存在紧张关系。题干中的share their parenting experiences对应定位句中的 parents’ rights to share their experiences，题干中的intruding into与定位句中的a tension still exists表达的意思一致，故答案为D）。

sections.title: Section C Passage 1
sections.passage:
1 Perhaps it is time for farmers to put their feet up now that robots are used to inspect crops, dig up weeds, and even have become shepherds, too.? 2 Commercial growing fields are astronomically huge and take thousands of man-hours to operate. 3 One prime example is one of Australia ’s most isolated cattle stations, Suplejack Downs in the Northern Territory, extending across 4,000 square kilometers, taking over 13 hours to reach by car from the nearest major town —— Alice Springs.
1 The extreme isolation of these massive farms leaves them often unattended, and monitored only once or twice a year, which means if the livestock falls ill or requires assistance, it can be a long time for farmers to discover.
1 However, robots are coming to the rescue.
1 Robots are currently under a two-year trial in Wales which will train ‘ farmbots ’ to herd, monitor the health of livestock, and make sure there is enough pasture for them to graze on.? 2 The robots are equipped with many sensors to identify conditions of the environment, cattle and food, using thermal and vision sensors that detect changes in body temperature.
1 “You’ve also got color, texture and shape sensors looking down at the ground to check pasture quality,” says Salah Sukkarieh of the University of Sydney, who will carry out trials on several farms in central New South Wales.
1 During the trials, the robot algorithms （算法） and mechanics will be fine-tuned to make it better suited to ailing livestock and ensure it safely navigates around potential hazards including trees, mud, swamps, and hills.
1 “We want to improve the quality of animal health and make it easier for farmers to maintain large landscapes where animals roam free,” says Sukkarieh.
1 The robots are not limited to herding and monitoring livestock. 2 They have been created to count individual fruit, inspect crops, and even pull weeds.
1 Many robots are equipped with high-tech sensors and complex learning algorithms to avoid injuring humans as they work side by side.? 2 The robots also learn the most efficient and safest passages, and allow engineers and farmers to analyze and better optimize the attributes and tasks of the robot, as well as provide a live stream giving real-time feedback on exactly what is happening on the farms.
1 Of course, some worry lies in replacing agricultural workers. 2 However, it is farmers that are pushing for the advancements due to ever-increasing labor vacancies, making it difficult to maintain large-scale operations.?
1 The robots have provided major benefits to farmers in various ways, from hunting and pulling weeds to monitoring the condition of every single fruit. 2 Future farms will likely experience a greater deal of autonomy as robots take up more and more farm work efficiently.?

questions.explanation:
【题干及选项概览】

What may farmers be able to do with robots appearing on the farming scene?

随着机器人出现在农耕场景中，农民能够做些什么？

A) Upgrade farm produce.

升级农场的产品

B) Enjoy more leisure hours.

享受休息的时间

C) Modify the genes of crops.

修改农作物的基因

D) Cut down farming costs.

削减农业生产成本

 

【定位及答案】

What can robots do when equipped with high-tech sensors and complex learning algorithms?

故答案为A）。

sections.passage:
1 The public must be able to understand the basics of science to make informed decisions. 2 Perhaps the most dramatic example of the negative consequences of poor communication between scientists and the public is the issue of climate change, where a variety of factors, not the least of which is a breakdown in the transmission of fundamental climate data to the general public, has contributed to widespread mistrust and misunderstanding of scientists and their research.?
1 The issue of climate change also illustrates how the public acceptance and understanding of science (or the lack of it) can influence governmental decision-making with regard to regulation, science policy and research funding.
1 However, the importance of effective communication with a general audience is not limited to hot issues like climate change. 2 It is also critical for socially charged neuroscience issues such as the genetic basis for a particular behavior, the therapeutic potential of stem cell therapy for neurodegenerative diseases, or the use of animal models, areas where the public understanding of science can also influence policy and funding decisions. 3 Furthermore, with continuing advances in individual genome （基因组） sequencing and the advent of personalized medicine, more non-scientists will need to be comfortable analyzing complex scientific information to make decisions that directly affect their quality of life.?
1 Science journalism is the main channel for the popularization of scientific information among the public. 2 Much has been written about how the relationship between scientists and the media can shape the efficient transmission of scientific advances to the public.? 3 Good science journalists are specialists in making complex topics accessible to a general audience, while adhering to scientific accuracy.
1 Unfortunately, pieces of science journalism can also oversimplify and generalize their subject material to the point that the basic information conveyed is obscured or at worst, obviously wrong.? 2 The impact of a basic discovery on human health can be exaggerated so that the public thinks a miraculous cure is a few months to years away when in reality the significance of the study is far more limited.
1 Even though scientists play a part in transmitting information to journalists and ultimately the public, too often the blame for ineffective communication is placed on the side of the journalists. 2 We believe that at least part of the problem lies in places other than the interaction between scientists and members of the media, and exists because for one thing we underestimate how difficult it is for scientists to communicate effectively with a diversity of audiences, and for another most scientists do not receive formal training in science communication.?

What should scientists do to impart their latest findings to the public more effectively?

提升他们的沟通技巧

由题干中的scientists do to impart和effectively 定位到文章最后一段①句和②句后半部分。定位段首句指出，尽管科学家在向新闻工作者和最终向公众传递信息方面起到了作用，但通常都把无效沟通归咎于新闻工作者这边。作者分析了他认为的两个真正原因：一方面是因为我们低估了科学家与各色受众进行有效沟通的难度，另一方面是因为大多数科学家没有接受过科学沟通的正规培训。D）所述建议与第二条原因相吻合，故为答案。

Do you mind taking my photo with the statue over there? I think it will make a great shot.
Sure, no worries. You’re always taking photos.
What do you do with all the photos you take?
Well, don’t laugh. My dream is to become an online celebrity of sorts.
You are not serious, are you?
I am, completely. I just got the idea a few months ago after posting some holiday photos on my social media accounts.
A lot of people liked my photos and started asking me for travel tips.
So I figured I’d give it a go. I post a lot on social media anyway.
So I’ve got nothing to lose.
I guess that’s true. So what do you have to do to become Internet famous?
Surprisingly a lot more than I did as a hobby.
Recently, I’ve been spending a lot more time editing photos, posting online and clearing storage on my phone.
It’s always full now.
That doesn’t sound like too much work.
Well, there’s more to it.
I spent all last weekend researching what topics are popular, what words to use in captions and similar accounts to follow.
It really was a lot to take in. And I was up well past midnight.
I’d say it’s paying off though.
I increased the number of people following m y accounts by 15% already.
That is impressive. I guess I never thought much about all the effort behind the scene.
Now that I think about it, there’s always something wrong with my photos as it is-half smiles, closed eyes, messy hair.
I hope you have better luck than I do.
Then again, I think the only person interested in my photos is my mom.

Good evening and welcome to Physics Today.
Here we interview some of the greatest minds in physics as they help us to understand some of the most complicated theories.
Today, I’m very pleased to welcome Dr. Melissa Phillips, professor of theoretical physics.
She’s here to tell us a little about what it is she studies. Dr. Phillips, you seem to study everything.
I guess that would be fair to say I spent most of my time studying the big bang theory and where our universe came from.
Can you tell us a little about that?
Well, I’m very interested in why the universe exists at all.
That may sound odd, but the fact is at the moment of the Big Bang, both matter and anti-matter were created for a short time, and I mean just a fraction of a second.
The whole universe was a super-hot soup of radiation filled with these particles.
So what’s baffled scientists for so long is “why is there a universe at all?”
That’s because matter and anti-matter are basically opposites of each other.
They are exactly alike except that they have opposite electrical charges.
So when they collide, they destroy each other?
Exactly. So during the first few moments of the Big Bang, the universe was extremely hot and very small.
Matter and the now more exotic anti-matter would have had little space to avoid each other.
This means that they should have totally wiped each other out, leaving the universe completely barren.
But a recent study seems to point to the fact that when matter and anti-matter were first created, there were slightly more particles of matter, which allowed the universe we all live in to form?
Exactly. Because there was slightly more matter, the collisions quickly depleted all the anti-matter and left just enough matter to create stars, planets and eventually us.

In this week’s edition of special series on Bizarre Medical Conditions, there is a report of the case of Michelle Myers.
Myers is an American woman who woke up one day speaking with a British accent, even though she’s lived in the United States all her life.
In 2015, Myers went to bed with a terrible headache.
She woke up sounding like someone from England.
Her British accent has remained for the past two years.
Previously, Myers had woken up speaking in Irish and Australian accents.
However, on both of those occasions, the accents lasted for only a week.
Myers has been diagnosed with Foreign Accent Syndrome.
It’s a disorder in which a person experiences a sudden change to their speech so that they sound like they’re speaking in a foreign accent.
The condition is most often caused by a stroke or traumatic brain injury.
Although people with the syndrome have intelligible speech, their manner of speaking is altered in terms of timing and tongue placement, which may distort their pronunciation.
The result is that they may sound foreign when speaking their native language.
It’s not clear whether Myers has experienced a stroke or other brain damage, but she also has a separate medical condition, which can result in loose joints, easily bruised skin and other problems.
Foreign Accent Syndrome is rare, with only about 60 cases reported within the past century.
However, a different American woman reportedly spoke with the Russian accent in 2010 after she fell down the stairs and hit her head.

There is something about water that makes it a good metaphor for life.
That may be one reason why so many people find relief in swimming when life's seas get rough.
And it goes some way towards explaining why books about swimming, in which people tackle icy lakes, race in rivers and overcome oceans while reflecting on their lives, have recently become so popular.
These books reflect a trend, particularly strong in Britain, where swimming in pools is declining, but more and more folks are opting for open water.
“Wild swimming” seems to be especially popular among women.
Jenny Landreth recently published a guide to the best swimming spots in London.
Her new book, Swell, interweaves her own story with a history of female pioneers who accomplished remarkable feats and paved the way for future generations.
Notions of modesty restricted women in the Victorian era, but they still swam.
A “bathing machine” was rolled down to the seashore so women would not be seen in swimwear.
In 1892, The Gentlewoman’s Book of Sport described a woman swimming in a heavy dress, boots, hat, gloves and carrying an umbrella.
Eventually, swimming became freer. Mixed bathing was permitted on British beaches in 1901.
Women won the right to swim in public pools, learned to swim properly, created appropriate swimwear and, in time, even competed against men.
The first woman to cross the English Channel was Gertrude Ederle in 1926.
She beat the record by almost two hours and her father rewarded her with a red sports car.

Today I’m going to talk about a very special kind of person.
Psychologists call them “masters of deception,” those rare individuals with a natural ability to tell with complete confidence when someone is telling a lie.
For decades, researchers and law enforcement agencies have tried to build a machine that will do the same thing.
Now a company in Massachusetts says that by using magnetic brain scans they can determine with 97% accuracy whether someone is telling the truth.
They hope that the technology will be cleared for use in American courts by early next year.
But is this really the ultimate tool for you, the lawyers of tomorrow?
You’ll not find many brain scientists celebrating this breakthrough.
The company might be very optimistic, but the ability of their machine to detect deception has not provided credible proof.
That’s because the technology has not been properly tested in real-world situations.
In life, there are different kinds of lies and diverse context in which they’re told.
These differences may elicit different brain responses.
Does their hypothesis behind the test apply in every case?
We don't know the answer, because studies done on how reliable this machine is have not yet been duplicated.
Much more research is badly needed.
Whether the technology is eventually deemed reliable enough for the courts will ultimately be decided by the judges.
Let’s hope they're wise enough not to be fooled by a machine that claims to determine truthfulness at the flick of a switch.
They should also be sceptical of the growing tendency to try to reduce all human traits and actions to the level of brain activity.
Often, they do not map that easily.
Moreover, understanding the brain is not the same as understanding the mind.
Some researchers have suggested that thoughts cannot properly be seen as purely “internal.”
Instead, thoughts make sense only in reference to the individual's external world.
So while there may be insights to be gained from matching behavior to brain activity, those insights will not necessarily lead to justice in a court of law.
Problems surround the use of machines to spot deception, at least until it has been rigorously tested.
A high-tech test that can tell when a person is not telling the truth sounds too good to be true.
And when something sounds too good to be true, it usually is.

Last week I attended a research workshop on an island in the South Pacific.
Thirty people were present and all except me came from the island, called Makelua, in the nation of Vanuatu.
They live in 16 different communities and speak 16 distinct languages.
In many cases, you could stand at the edge of one village and see the outskirts of the next community.
Yet the residents of each village speak a completely different language.
According to recent work by my colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History, this island, just 100 kilometers long and 20 kilometers wide, is home to speakers of perhaps 40 different indigenous languages.
Why so many? We could ask the same question of the entire globe.
People don't speak one universal language, or even a handful.
Instead, today our species collectively speaks over 7,000 distinct languages, and these languages are not spread randomly across the planet.
For example, far more languages are found in tropical regions than in the mild zones.
The tropical island of New Guinea is home to over 900 languages.
Russia,20 times larger, has 105 indigenous languages.
Even within the tropics, language diversity varies widely.
For example, the 250,00 people who live on Vanuatu’s 80 islands speak 110 different languages, but in Bangladesh, a population 600 times greater speaks only 41 languages.
How come humans speak so many languages?
And why are they so unevenly spread across the planet?
As it turns out. we have few clear answers to these fundamental questions about how humanity communicates.
Most people can easily brainstorm possible answers to these intriguing questions.
They hypothesize that language diversity must be about history, cultural differences, mountains or oceans dividing populations.
But when our diverse team of researchers from six different disciplines and eight different countries began to review what was known, we were shocked that only a dozen previous studies had been done, including one we ourselves completed on language diversity in the Pacific.
These prior efforts all examined the degree to which different environmental, social and geographic variables correlated with the number of languages found in a given location.
The results varied a lot from one study to another, and no clear patterns emerged.
The studies also ran up against many methodological challenges, the biggest of which centered on the old statistical saying—correlation does not equal causation.

We often hear people say that America is a land of opportunity, a country built on hope to aspire the greatness on the American dream.
But is the dream as we once knew it dying?
Today’s demographics show that the middle-class is disappearing and now the richest 1% of the population has mastered more wealth than the bottom 90%.
Once upon a time, Americans thought that if they worked hard enough, even in the phase of adversity, they would be rewarded with success.
These days, though, the divide between rich and poor is greater than it has ever been.
The question is, what is it going to take to change things?
Maybe one day soon, real change will actually be made in our nation and the gap will be eradicated.
But what happens in the meantime?
Is there something that we can do to help close the gap?
Is there something that we can do to prove that a little compassion goes a long way?
If we want to fix the problem of the income gap, first, we have to understand it.
It is a grim reality that you can have one person who only makes around $13,000 a year, or across town, another is making millions.
For me, it is kind of astonishing.
And if you ask low-income people what’s the one thing that will change their life, they'll say “a full-time job.”
That's all they aspire to.
So why is it so difficult for so many people to find employment?
It partly comes down to profit-driven business models that are built around low-wage work and part-time jobs that don't provide benefits.
Businesses, in order to boost profits, hire employees as part-time workers only.
This means they are paid the lowest legal wage and receive no health care or other benefits provided to full-time employees.
Simultaneously, technological advancement and a global economy has reduced the demand for well-paying blue-collar jobs here in the United States.
The cumulative effect of these two factors is that many Americans are forced to take two or more part-time jobs, just to make ends meet.
What has become obvious to me when it comes to the income gap is that there needs to be an opportunity for the people at the bottom to push them back up and push them into the middle-class to give them hope in their lives.

1 In today’s highly competitive environment, the heavy workload makes people out of breath and leaves them no time for their hobbies. 2 Therefore, learning to balance job responsibilities and personal interests is of great significance for modern people.
1 Here are some suggestions which can help us achieve the balance. 2 In the first place, we should be aware that although work duties are our first priority, it doesn't mean that we cannot explore personal interests. 3 Secondly, it’s important to realize that beneficial activities off work help us get relaxed. 4 We can transfer our focus from busy work to an interesting book or to music, thereby getting our intense nerves calm down. 5 What’s more, find enough time to develop our hobbies by finishing the task on time. 6 We should arrange our time reasonably and complete our daily work efficiently, which will give us more freedom to allocate time to pursue personal interests.
1 In sum, it is absolutely do-able to strike a balance between full-time work and personal hobbies as long as we realize the benefit of cultivating interests and the importance of reasonable time arrangement.

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格前面为struggling to, struggle的常见用法为struggle to do sth.“挣扎着做（困难的）事”，这里的to为不定式符号，因此空格应填入动词原形。

【答案解析】

由空格所在句可知，在课上上网会伤害一些学生，空格前的already暗示这些学生本就已经对课堂内容理解有困难，故填入F）grasp“理解，领悟”。下一句中的though表明两句之间暗含转折关系，该句表明所有学生——包括成绩优异的学生——在课上出于非学习目的上网浏览时，学习成绩都会下降。也就是说，在课上上网不仅会影响学习，有理解困难的学生还会影响包括成绩优异的学生在内的所有学生，由此也可推出答案。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于主语researchers和宾语students之间，应填入动词作谓语。本段的主要时态为一般过去时，故填入动词的过去式。

【答案解析】

由空格所在句可知，为了衡量上课期间上网对分散学生注意力的影响，研究人员________密歇根州立大学上心理学入门课的500名学生。由常识可知，在实验研究中，要衡量某种影响的话，一般要对受试者进行评估或测验，故填入C）evaluated“评估，评价”。

【考点】

名词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格所在介词短语of intellectual ________作a measure的后置定语，应填入名词。

【答案解析】

空格前的形容词intellectual意为“智力的”，结合备选名词，它应该用来修饰aptitude，指智力资质，即研究人员用美国大学入学考试的成绩作为衡量智力资质的标准，故填入A）aptitude“天资，天赋”

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于短语are better at之后，应填入动词的现在分词构成固定搭配，且所填词可以与后面的out搭配。

【答案解析】

be better at doing sth. 意为“擅长做某事”，空格后的distractions意为“让人分心的事物”，可推出应该是擅长把不好的东西除掉，故填入E）filtering“过滤”。filter out意为“过滤掉”。

【考点】

形容词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于冠词a和名词decrease之间，应填入形容词修饰名词。

【答案解析】

由句意可知，空格处要填入一个表程度的形容词修饰 decrease。空格所在句与下一句之间用But连接表示转折。空格所在句表明，研究人员本以为入学考试分数高的学生不会因为使成绩下滑。下一句指用数码产品而出现________成绩下滑。下一句指出，无论他们的入学考试的成绩如何，那些在课上上网的学生确实在测试中表现更差。综上可知，应填入M）significant“影响明显的”。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于助动词are和副词之后，应填入动词的-ing形式构成现在进行时。

【答案解析】

根据下一段内容可知，高校教授们为减少学生课上使用数码产品的情况会执行一些政策。空格后的alarm bells意为“警钟，警告”，由此推测这里指高校教授们“提出”警示，故填入K）raising“提出，提起”。

【考点】

形容词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于冠词a和名词class之间，应填入形容词。

【答案解析】

本句陈述研究结果：平均每个学生在一堂________课上查看数码产品11次。根据常识可知，这是一个普遍现象，故填入O）typical“平常的，一贯的”。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于cause sth.to结构之后，这里的to是不定式符号，因此空格应填入动词原形。

【答案解析】

文章一直在讲课上使用数码产品对学生成绩造成的负面影响，因此这里应填入N）suffer“变差”。H）minimize虽然有“把……减至最小量”的意思，但它是及物动词，后面需要跟宾语，故排除。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格前的to为不定式符号，因此空格应填入动词原形。

【答案解析】

本句中的designed to…是过去分词短语作后置定语，修饰前面的policies，表目的。由and后提到的“有些讲师甚至会没收���板电脑和手机”可知，这些政策是为了减少或消除学生课上使用数码产品，故填入H）minimize“把……减至最小量”。

【考点】

动词辨析题。

【确定词性】

空格位于are able to之后，需填入动词原形。

【答案解析】

Until引导的从句表示条件，空格后的宾语pull在此处意为“吸引力，诱惑”。该句意为，除非学生能________社交网络、短信以及无休止地浏览网页所带来的诱惑，否则他们可能会继续在课上苦苦挣扎。也就是说，只有抵挡住这些诱惑，他们才可能不会挣扎，故填入L）resist“抵挡，忍住”。

sections.title: Section B 快速阅读
sections.passage:
1 Maria Sibylla Merian, like many European women of the 17th century, stayed busy managing a household and rearing children. 2 But on top of that, Merian, a German-born woman who lived in the Netherlands, also managed a successful career as an artist, botanist, naturalist and entomologist（昆虫学家）.
1 “She was a scientist on the level with a lot of people we spend a lot of time talking about,” said Kay Etheridge, a biologist at Gettysburg College in Pennsylvania who has been studying the scientific history of Merian’s work. 2 “She didn't do as much to change biology as Charles Darwin, but she was significant.”
1 At a time when natural history was a valuable tool for discovery, Merian discovered facts about plants and insects that were not previously known. 2 Her observations helped dismiss the popular belief that insects spontaneously emerged from mud. 3 The knowledge she collected over decades didn’t just satisfy those curious about nature, but also provided valuable insights into medicine and science. 4 She was the first to bring together insects and their habitats, including food they ate, into a single ecological composition.?
1 After years of pleasing a fascinated audience across Europe with books of detailed descriptions and life-size paintings of familiar insects, in 1699 she sailed with her daughter nearly 5,000 miles from the Netherlands to South America to study insects in the jungles of what is now known as Suriname. 2 She was 52 years old. 3 The result was her masterpiece, Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium.?
1 In her work, she revealed a side of nature so exotic, dramatic and valuable to Europeans of the time that she received much acclaim. 2 But a century later, her findings came under scientific criticism. 3 Shoddy（粗糙的）reproductions of her work along with setbacks to women's roles in 18th- and 19th-century Europe resulted in her efforts being largely forgotten. 4 “It was kind of stunning when she sort of dropped off into oblivion（遗忘）, ”said Dr. Etheridge. 5 “Victorians started putting women in a box, and they're still trying to crawl out of it.”?
1 Today, the pioneering woman of the sciences has re-emerged. 2 In recent years, feminists, historians and artists have all praised Merian’s tenacity（坚韧）, talent and inspirational artistic compositions. 3 And now biologists like Dr. Etheridge are digging into the scientific texts that accompanied her art. 4 Three hundred years after her death, Merian will be celebrated at an international symposium in Amsterdam this June.?
1 And last month, Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium was republished. 2 It contains 60 plates（插图）and original descriptions, along with stories about Merian’s life and updated scientific descriptions. 3 Before writing Metamorphosis, Merian spent decades documenting European plants and insects that she published in a series of books. 4 She began in her 20s, making textless, decorative paintings of flowers with insects. 5 “Then she got really serious,” Dr. Etheridge said. 6 Merian started raising insects at home, mostly butterflies and caterpillars. 7 “She would sit up all night until they came out of the pupa （蛹） so she could draw them,” she said.?
1 The results of her decades’ worth of careful observations were detailed paintings and descriptions of European insects, followed by unconventional visuals and stories of insects and animals from a land that most at the time could only imagine. 2 It’s possible Merian used a magnifying glass to capture the detail of the split tongues of sphinx moths（斯芬克斯飞蛾）depicted in the painting. 3 She wrote that the two tongues combine to form one tube for drinking nectar（花蜜）. 4 Some criticized this detail later, saying there was just one tongue, but Merian wasn’t wrong. 5 She may have observed the adult moth just as it emerged from its pupa. 6 For a brief moment during that stage of its life cycle, the tongue consists of two tiny half-tubes before merging into one.
1 It may not have been ladylike to depict a giant spider devouring a hummingbird, but when Merian did it at the turn of the 18th century, surprisingly, nobody objected. 2 Dr. Etheridge called it revolutionary. 3 The image, which also contained novel descriptions of ants, fascinated a European audience that was more concerned with the exotic story unfolding before them than the gender of the person who painted it.
1 “All of these things shook up their nice, neat little view,” Dr. Etheridge said. 2 But later, people of the Victorian era thought differently. 3 Her work had been reproduced, sometimes incorrectly. 4 A few observations were deemed impossible. 5 “She’d been called a silly woman for saying that a spider could eat a bird,” Dr. Etheridge said. 6 But Henry Walter Bates, a friend of Charles Darwin, observed it and put it in book in 1863, proving Merian was correct.
1 In the same plate, Merian depicted and described leaf-cutter ants for the first time. 2 “In America there are large ants which can eat whole trees bare as a broom handle in a single night,” she wrote in the description. 3 Merian noted how the ants took the leaves below ground to their young. 4 And she wouldn’t have known this at the time, but the ants use the leaves to farm fungi（菌类）underground to feed their developing babies.?
1 Merian was correct about the giant bird-eating spiders, ants building bridges with their bodies and other details. 2 But in the same drawing, she incorrectly lumped together army and leaf-cutter ants. 3 And instead of showing just the typical pair of eggs in a hummingbird nest, she painted four. 4 She made other mistakes in Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium as well: not every caterpillar and butterfly matched.?
1 Perhaps one explanation for her mistakes is that she cut short her Suriname trip after getting sick, and completed the book at home in Amsterdam. 2 And errors are common among some of history’s most-celebrated scientific minds, too. 3 “These errors no more invalidate Ms. Merian’s work than do well-known misconceptions published by Charles Darwin or Isaac Newton,” Dr. Etheridge wrote in a paper that argued that too many have wrongly focused on the mistakes of her work.?
1 Merian’s paintings inspired artists and ecologists. 2 In an 1801 drawing from his book, General Zoology Amphibia, George Shaw, an English botanist and zoologist, credited Merian for describing a frog in the account of her South American expedition, and named the young tree frog after her in his portrayal of it. 3 It wouldn't be fair to give Merian all the credit. 4 She received assistance naming plants, making sketches and referencing the work of others. 5 Her daughters helped her color her drawings.
1 Merian also made note of the help she received from the natives of Suriname, as well as slaves or servants that assisted her. 2 In some instances she wrote moving passages that included her helpers in descriptions. 3 As she wrote in her description of the peacock flower, “The Indians, who are not treated well by their Dutch masters, use the seeds to abort their children, so that they will not become slaves like themselves. 4 The black slaves from Guinea and Angola have demanded to be well treated, threatening to refuse to have children. 5 In fact, they sometimes take their own lives because they are treated so badly, and because they believe they will be born again, free and living in their own land. 6 They told me this themselves.”?
1 Londa Schiebinger, a professor of the history of science at Stanford University, called this passage rather astonishing. 2 It’s particularly striking centuries later when these issues are still prominent in public discussions about social justice and women's rights. 3 “She was ahead of her time,” Dr. Etheridge said.

questions.explanation:
【定位】

由题干关键词Merian、the first scientist和American ant定位到K）段前两句。

 

【答案解析】

细节归纳题。定位句提到，在同一幅插图里，梅里安首次绘制并描述了切叶蚁。紧接着第二句指出切叶蚁是一种美洲蚂蚁。题干中的study是对原文中depicted and described的总结，故答案为K）。

【定位】

由题干关键词The European audience和gender定位到I段画线处。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，这幅画中还包含了对蚂蚁的新颖描述，它吸引了欧洲读者，他们更关心的是展现在他们面前的奇异故事，而不是绘制者的性别。题干中的more interested in对应原文中的more concerned with，题干中的Merian’s drawings对应原文中的the exotic story unfolding before them，故答案为I。

【定位】

由题干关键词came under attack和a century after定位到E）段第二句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，一个世纪后，她的发现受到了科学界的批评。上一段最后一句提到了梅里安的著作《苏里南昆虫变态图谱》，由此可知，一个世纪之后，她的著作受到了抨击。题干中的came under attack对应原文中的came under scientific criticism，故答案为E）。

【定位】

由题干关键词Merian’s mistakes、be attributed to 和 her shortened stay in South America定位到M）段第一句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，或许有一点能解释她的错误：她生病后突然中断了苏里南之行，并在阿姆斯特丹的家中完成了这本书。题干中的may be attributed to对应原文中的Perhaps one explanation for，题干中的 her shortened stay in South America 对应原文中的she cut short her Suriname trip，故答案为M）。

【定位】

由题干关键词sat up the whole night through和draw insects定位到G）段最后一句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，她会彻夜不眠等到它们破蛹而出，以便描绘它们。根据上一句可知，定位句中的She就是指梅里安，而they指代昆虫。题干中的often sat up the whole night through对应原文中的would sit up all night，故答案为G）。

【定位】

由题干关键词the help及 natives of South America定位到O）段第一句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，梅里安还记录了她从苏里南土著那里获得的帮助，以及曾经帮过她的奴隶或仆人。由上文可知，苏里南位于南美洲。题干中的acknowledged对应原文中的 made note of，故答案为 O）。

【定位】

由题干关键词people’s better understanding和medicine and science定位到C）段第三句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，她几十年来收集的知识不仅满足了那些对自然好奇的人，而且为医学和科学提供了宝贵的见解。也就是说，她几十年来收集的知识为人们更好地了解医学和科学作出了巨大的贡献。题干中的people’s better understanding对应原文中的valuable insights，故答案为C）。

【定位】

由题干关键词occasionally made mistakes和drawings of insects and birds定位到L）段。

 

【答案解析】

细节归纳题。定位段第一句提到，梅里安关于巨型食鸟蜘蛛、用身体搭桥的蚂蚁以及其他细节的看法是正确的。但紧接着举了三个例子说明她在昆虫和鸟类的绘画上出现的错误：在同一幅画中，她把行军蚁和切叶蚁错误地混在了一起；在一个蜂鸟巢中画了四颗鸟蛋；《苏里南昆虫变态图谱》中的毛虫和蝴蝶不能完全一一对应。由此可知，梅里安的大部分看法是正确的，但她偶尔会在昆虫和鸟类的绘画上出错。题干是对定位段的概括，故答案为L）。

【定位】

由题干关键词a female forerunner in sciences和 re-established定位到F）段第一句。

 

【答案解析】

同义转述题。定位句提到，如今，这位科学界的先驱女性已重新亮相。由上下文可知，此处的科学界的先驱女性就是指梅里安。题干中female forerunner 对应原文中的the pioneering woman；题干中的re-established对应原文中的re-emerged。题干是对定位句的同义转述，故答案为F）。

【定位】

由题干关键词South America, study jungle insects和over three centuries ago定位到D）段第一句。

 

【答案解析】

细节推断题。定位句后半部分提到，她于1699年和女儿一起从荷兰航行了将近5,000英里到达南美洲，去研究如今被称为苏里南丛林中的昆虫。题干中的made a long voyage to South America是对原文中sailed...nearly 5,000 miles from the Netherlands to South America的概括，题干中的over three centuries ago对应原文中的in 1699（1699年距今超过三个世纪），故答案为D）。

sections.title: Section C Passage 1
sections.passage:
1 While human achievements in mathematics continue to reach new levels of complexity, many of us who aren’t mathematicians at heart (or engineers by trade) may struggle to remember the last time we used calculus （微积分）.?
1 It’s a fact not lost on American educators, who amid rising math failure rates are debating how math can better meet the real-life needs of students. 2 Should we change the way math is taught in schools, or eliminate some courses entirely?
1 Andrew Hacker, Queens College political science professor, thinks that advanced algebra and other higher-level math should be cut from curricula in favor of courses with more routine usefulness, like statistics.
1 “We hear on all sides that we’re not teaching enough mathematics, and the Chinese are running rings around us,” Hacker says.? 2 “I’m suggesting we’re teaching too much mathematics to too many people... not everybody has to know calculus. 3 If you’re going to become an aeronautical （航空的） engineer, fine. 4 But most of us aren’t.”
1 Instead, Hacker is pushing for more courses like the one he teaches at Queens College: Numeracy 101. 2 There, his students of “citizen statistics” learn to analyze public information like the federal budget and corporate reports. 3 Such courses, Hacker argues, are a remedy for the numerical illiteracy of adults who have completed high-level math like algebra but are unable to calculate the price of, say, a carpet by area.?
1 Hacker’s argument has met with opposition from other math educators who say what’s needed is to help students develop a better relationship with math earlier, rather than teaching them less math altogether.
1 Maria Droujkova is a founder of Natural Math, and has taught basic calculus concepts to 5-year-olds. 2 For Droujkova, high-level math is important, and what it could use in American classrooms is an injection of childlike wonder.
1 “Make mathematics more available,” Droujkova says.? 2 “Redesign it so it’s more accessible to more kinds of people: young children, adults who worry about it, adults who may have had bad experiences.”
1 Pamela Harris, a lecturer at the University of Texas at Austin, has a similar perspective. 2 Harris says that American education is suffering from an epidemic of “fake math” —— an emphasis on rote memorization （死记硬背） of formulas and steps, rather than an understanding of how math can influence the ways we see the world.?
1 Andrew Hacker, for the record, remains skeptical.
1 “I’m going to leave it to those who are in mathematics to work out the ways to make their subject interesting and exciting so students want to take it,” Hacker says. 2 “All that I ask is that alternatives be offered instead of putting all of us on the road to calculus.”

questions.explanation:
【题干及选项概览】

What does the author say about ordinary Americans?

关于普通美国人，作者说了什么？

A) They struggle to solve math problems.

他们努力解决数学问题

B) They think math is a complex subject.

他们认为数学是一门复杂的学科

C) They find high-level math of little use.

他们发现高等数学用处不大

D) They work hard to learn high-level math.

他们努力学习高等数学

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的the author 和ordinary Americans定位到文章1段。定位段指出，虽然人类数学成就的复杂性持续再创新高，但我们当中许多本身并非数学家（或者职业并非工程师）的人，可能很难记起我们上一次使用微积分是什么时候了，也就是说，许多美国人很少使用微积分，发现高等数学的用处不大，故答案为C）。

 

【错误选项分析】

A选项【反向干扰】：定位段提到我们当中许多人可能很难记起我们上一次使用微积分是什么时候了，并不是说许多美国人在努力解决数学问题，可以排除A）“他们努力解决数学问题”；

B选项【答非所问】：定位段提到人类数学成就的复杂性持续再创新高，这是描述现实情况，而不是表示普通美国民众的观点，可以排除B）“他们认为数学是一门复杂的学科”；

D选项【无中生有】：原文并未提到作者认为普通美国民众努力学习高等数学，可以排除D）“他们努力学习高等数学”。

questions.explanation:
【题干及选项概览】

What is the general complaint about America’s math education according to Hacker?

哈克对美国数学教育的普遍抱怨是什么？

A) America is not doing as well as China.

美国的数学教育不如中国

B) Math professors are not doing a good job.

数学教授们做得不好

C) It doesn’t help students develop their literacy.

这并不能帮助学生培养他们的读写能力

D) There has hardly been any innovation for years.

数年来儿乎没有任何创新

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的general complaint、America’s math education和Hacker 定位到文章4段①句。定位句指出，哈克说各方都认为美国没有教授足够的数学知识，而中国人远胜过美国人。也就是说，哈克认为人们普遍抱怨的是美国的数学教育不如中国，故答案为A）。

 

【错误选项分析】

B选项【偷换概念】：定位句提到各方都说我们没有教授足够的数学知识，这里“教学的主体”泛指数学教育工作者，并没有特指数学教授，B）“数学教授们做得不好”是对原文的误解，可以排除；

C选项【词汇干扰】：5段最后一句提到了the numerical illiteracy，指出像“算术101”这种课程对于缺乏算术能力的成年人来说是一种补救措施，但并未提到美国的数学教育能否语助学生培养他们的读写能力，可以排除C）“这并不能帮助学生培养他们的读写能力”；

D选项【无中生有】：文中没有提到美国数学教育的创新问题，可以排除D）“数年来儿乎没有任何创新”

【题干及选项概览】

What does Andrew Hacker’s Numeracy 101 aim to do?

Andrew Hacker的“算术101“课程旨在做什么？

A) Allow students to learn high-level math step by step.

让学生循序渐进地学习高等数学

B) Enable students to make practical use of basic math.

让学生能够在实践中运用基础数学

C) Lay a solid foundation for advanced math studies.

为高等数学的学习打下坚实的基础

D) Help students to develop their analytical abilities.

帮助学生培养他们的分析能力

【定位及答案】

根据题干中的Numeracy 101定位到文章4段①句和③句。定位句指出，哈克正在争取开设更多像“算数101”的课程，他认为这种课程对于缺乏算数能力的成年人来说是一种补教措施，他们虽然学完了像代数这样的高等数学，但却不会按面积计算一张地毯的价格。也就是说，安德鲁·哈克的“算数101”课程旨在让学生能够在实践中运用基础数学，故答案为B）。

【错误选项分析】

A/C选项【反向干扰】：4段③句提到，像“算数101”这种课程对于缺乏算数能力的成年人来说是一种补救措施，而且这些人已经学完了像代数这样的高等教学。由此可知，这门课程只是补救措施，而不是让学生循序渐进地学习高等数学或者为高等数学的学习打下基础，可以排除A）“让学生循序渐进地学习高等数学”和C）“为高等数学的学习打下坚实的基础”；

D选项【偷换概念】：4段②句虽然提到在这门课程里，学习“公民统计”的学生学习分析公共信息，但这门课程的目的并非培养学生的分析能力，而是提高他们的实用数学能力，可以排除D）“帮助学生培养他们的分析能力”。

【题干及选项概览】

What does Maria Droujkova suggest math teachers do in class?

Maria Droujkova建议数学老师们在课堂中做什么？

A) Make complex concepts easy to understand.

让复杂的概念容易理解

B) Start teaching children math at an early age.

在孩子们小的时候就开始教他们数学

C) Help children work wonders with calculus.

帮助孩子们用微积分创造奇迹

D) Try to arouse students’ curiosity in math.

尝试激发学生对数学的好奇心

【定位及答案】

由题干中的Maria Droujkova和suggest定位到7段。定位段着重描述德鲁伊科娃建议数学老师怎么做：让数学知识更易懂，重新设计数学，使其更容易被更多类型的人（年幼的孩子，为数学烦恼的成年人，可能有过相关糟糕经历的成年人）所理解。由此可知，德鲁伊科娃建议数学老师在课堂上要使复杂的概念容易理解，故答案为A）。

【错误选项分析】

B选项【答非所问】：6段①句提到德鲁伊科娃向5岁的儿童教授基本的微积分概念，但并未提到她建议数学老师在孩子们小的时候就开始教他们数学，可以排除B）“在孩子们小的时候就开始教他们数学”；

C选项【偷换概念】：6段②句指出，高等数学在美国课堂上的作用是注入孩童般的好奇心，而不是“帮助孩子们用微积分创造奇迹”，故排除C）

D选项【答非所问】：可以注入孩童般的好奇心是德鲁伊科娃对高数的用处的看法， 文中并没有提到她建议老师在课堂上D）“尝试激发学生对数学的好奇心”，故排除D）。

questions.explanation:
【题干及选项概览】

What does Pamela Harris think should be the goal of math education?

Pamela Harris认为什么应该是数学教育的目标？

A) To enable learners to understand the world better.

能让学习者更好的理解世界

B) To help learners to tell fake math from real math.

能够帮助学习这门区分真假数学

C) To broaden Americans’ perspectives on math.

去开拓美国人对于数学的认知角度

D) To exert influence on world development.

对世界的发展施加影响

【定位及答案】

由题干中的Pamela Harris和math education定位到8段②句。定位句指出，哈里斯表示，美国教育正在遭遇“虚假数学”的泛滥——强调死记硬背公式和步骤，而不是理解数学如何影响我们看待世界的方式。也就是说，哈里斯认为美国教育应该强调理解数学如何影响我们的观念，即让人们更好地理解数学这门学科，从更容易理解的角度讲数学，从而开拓美国人对数学的认知角度，故答案为C）。

【错误选项分析】

A选项【范围过大】：A）项干扰性较大，A）的概念太宽泛，定位句强调的是数学如何影响我们看待世界的方式，而不是更好地理解世界，故排除A）

B选项【过度推理】：定位句提到了美国教育正在遭遇“虚假数学”的泛滥，但并没有提及要区分真假数学，可以排除B）“帮助学习者区分真假数学”；

D选项【偷换概念】：定位句提到的是数学影响我们看待世界的方式，而不是影响世界的发展，可以排除D）“对世界的发展施加影响”。

sections.title: Section C Passage 2
sections.passage:
1 For years, the U.S. has experienced a shortage of registered nurses. 2 The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that while the number of nurses will increase by 19 percent by 2022, demand will grow faster than supply, and that there will be over one million unfilled nursing jobs by then.
1 So what’s the solution? 2 Robots.
1 Japan is ahead of the curve when it comes to this trend.? 2 Toyohashi University of Technology has developed Terapio, a robotic medical cart that can make hospital rounds, deliver medications and other items, and retrieve records. 3 It follows a specific individual, such as a doctor or nurse, who can use it to record and access patient data. 4 This type of robot will likely be one of the first to be implemented in hospitals because it has fairly minimal patient contact.?
1 Robots capable of social engagement help with loneliness as well as cognitive functioning, but the robot itself doesn’t have to engage directly —— it can serve as an intermediary for human communication. 2 Telepresence robots such as MantaroBot, Vgo, and Giraff can be controlled through a computer, smartphone, or tablet, allowing family members or doctors to remotely monitor patients or Skype them, often via a screen where the robot ’s ‘ face ’ would be.? 3 If you can’t get to the nursing home to visit grandma, you can use a telepresence robot to hang out with her. 4 A 2016 study found that users had a “consistently” positive attitude” about the Giraff robot ’s ability to enhance communication and decrease feeling of loneliness.
1 A robot’ s appearance affects its ability to successfully interact with humans, which is why the RIKEN-TRI Collaboration Center for Human-Interactive Robot Research decided to develop a robotic nurse that looks like a huge teddy bear. 2 RIBA (Robot for Interactive Body Assistance), also known as ' Robear ', can help patients into and out of wheelchairs and beds with its strong arms.
1 On the less cute and more scary side there is Actroid F, which is so human-like that some patients may not know the difference. 2 This conversational robot companion has cameras in its eyes, which allow it to track patients and use appropriate facial expressions and body language in its interactions.? 3 During a month-long hospital trial, researchers asked 70 patients how they felt being around the robot and “only three or four said they didn’t like having it around.”
1 It’s important to note that robotic nurses don't decide courses of treatment or make diagnoses (though robot doctors and surgeons may not be far off). 2 Instead, they perform routine and laborious tasks, freeing nurses up to attend to patients with immediate needs. 3 This is one industry where it seems the integration of robots will lead to collaboration, not replacement.?

【题干及选项概览】

What does the author say about Japan?

关于日本，作者说了什么？

A) It delivers the best medications for the elderly.

日本给老年人递送最好的药物

B) It takes the lead in providing robotic care.

日本在提供机器人护理方面处于领先地位

C) It provides retraining for registered nurses.

日本向注册护士提供再培训

D) It sets the trend in future robotics technology.

日本引领未来机器人技术的潮流

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的Japan定位到文章3段①句。定位句指出，就该潮流而言，日本处于领先地位。由上文可知，该潮流是指用机器人代替空缺护理岗位的潮流。也就是说，日本在提供机器人护理方面处于领先地位，B）选项中的takes the lead对应定位句中的 ahead of the curve，故答案为B）。

 

【错误选项分析】

A选项【偷换概念&无中生有】：3段②句提到，丰桥技术科学大学开发的一种机器人医用推车Terapio可以递送药物，而不是指日本递送药物，并且原文并未提及是向老年人递送最佳药物，可以排除A）“日本给老年人递送最好的药物”。

C选项【无中生有】：原文并未提及C）“日本向注册护士提供再培训”，可以排除。

D选项【曲解文意】：定位句是指日本引领目前的机器人护理潮流，而不是未来机器人技术的潮流，选项D）“日本引领未来机器人技术的潮流”是对原文的曲解，可以排除。

【题干及选项概览】

What do we learn about the robot Terapio?

关于Terapio我们知道什么？

A) It has been put to use in many Japanese hospitals.

Terapio已在许多家日本医院中投入使用

B) It provides specific individualized care to patients.

Terapio向患者提供特定的个性化护理

C) It does not have much direct contact with patients.

Terapio没有和患者有过多的接触

D) It has not revolutionized medical service in Japan.

Terapio并未彻底改革日本的医疗服务

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的Terapio定位到文章3段。定位段最后一句指出，这类机器人可能是最早在医院投入使用的机器人之一，因为它与患者的接触相当少。由3段②句可知，This type of robot就是指Terapio这类机器人，也就是说Terapio与患者的接触相当少，故答案为C）。

 

【错误选项分���】

A选项【无中生有】：定位句只提到Terapio这类机器人可能是最早一批在医院投入使用的机器人，并未提及使用Terapio的日本医院的数最，可以排除A）“Terapio已在许多家日本医院中投入使用”。

B选项【偷换概念】：3段③句提到Terapio跟随特定的个人，而不是向患者提供特定的个性化护理，可以排除B）“Terapio向患者提供特定的个性化护理”。

D选项【无中生有】：文中没有提到日本医疗服务的改革，可以排除D）“Terapio并未彻底改革日本的医疗服务”

【题干及选项概览】

What are telepresence robots designed to do?

远程呈现机器人是被设计用来做什么的？

A) Directly interact with patients to prevent them from feeling lonely.

与患者直接互动会防止他们感到孤独

B) Cater to the needs of patients for recovering their cognitive capacity.

满足患者恢复其认知能力的需求

C) Closely monitor the patients’ movements and conditions around the clock.

全天候密切监控患者的行动和状况

D) Facilitate communication between patients and doctors or family members.

被用来促进患者与医生或家人之间的交流

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的telepresence robots和designed定位到文章4段②句。定位句指出，诸如MantaroBot、Vgo和 Giraff等远程呈现机器人允许家人或医生远程监控患者或者使用Skype与患者聊天。也就是说，远程呈现机器人被用来促进患者与医生或家人之间的交流，故答案为D）。

 

【错误选项分析】

A选项【反向干扰】：4段①句提到机器人本身不必直接参与社交，它可以作为人类交流的中介，定位句也指出家人或医生通过远程呈现机器人远程监控患者或者使用Skype与患者聊天。由此可知，远程呈现机器人不会与患者直接互动，可以排除A）“与患者直接互动会防止他们感到孤独”

B选项【过度推理】：4段①句只提到能够进行社交的机器人有助于缓解病人的孤独感和提升认知功能，但并未提及能恢复患者的认知能力，可以排除B）“满足患者恢复其认知能力的需求”。

C选项【过度推理】：定位句虽然提到远程呈现机器允许家人或医生远程监控患者，但并未提及要全天候地密切监控，可以排除C）“全天候密切监控患者的���动和状况”。

【题干及选项概览】

What is one special feature of the robot Actroid F?

机器人Actroid F的一个特别之处是什么？

A) It interacts with patients just like a human companion.

它会像人类伴侣一样与患者进行互动

B) It operates quietly without patients realizing its presence.

它运行时非常安静，患者都意识不到它的存在

C) It likes to engage in everyday conversations with patients.

它喜欢与患者进行日常对话

D) It uses body language even more effectively than words.

它使用肢体语言甚至比使用言语更有效

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的Actroid F定位到文意6段①②句。定位句指出，Actroid F与人类如此相似，以至于一些思者可能不清楚其区别，歌接着第二句对Actroid F的这一特点进行了详细的解释：这种会话式机器人伴倡的眼睛里有摄像头，可以跟踪患者，并在交流中使用适当的面部表情和肢体语言。由此可知，Actroid F的一个特别之处是它会像人类伴侣一样与患者进行互动，故答案为A）。

 

【错误选项分析】

B选项【反向干扰】：6段②句提到Actroid F与患者交流，就然是交流，患者肯定意识到了Actroid F的存在，可以排除B）“它运行时非常安静，患者都意识不到它的存在”。

C选项【偷换概念】：与患者交流是ActroidF的功能，而不是它的喜好，可以排除C）“它喜欢与患者进行日常对话”。

D选项【无中生有】：6段②句虽然提到Actroid F在交流中使用适当的面部表情和肢体语言，但并未将肢体语言和言语的效果进行比较，可以排除D）“它使用肢体语言甚至比使用言语更有效”。

questions.explanation:
【题干及选项概览】

What can we infer from the last paragraph?

根据最后一段我们可以推知什么？

A) Doctors and surgeons will soon be laid off

医生和外科医生很快就会下岗

B) The robotics industry will soon take off.

机器人行业不久之后就会腾飞

C) Robots will not make nurses redundant.

机器人不会导致护士们被解雇

D) Collaboration will not replace competition.

合作不会取代竞争

 

【定位及答案】

由题干中的the last paragraph定位到7段。7段①句指出，机器人护士不会决定治疗过程或作出诊断，紧接着②句表明它们执行常规且费时费力的任务，让护士有更多的时间去照顾有急需的患者，③句总结指出在护土行业中机器人的融入将带来合作而非替代。也就是说，机器人与护土是合作而非替代的关系，它们并不会导致护士们被解雇，故答案为C）。

 

【错误选项分析】

A选项【反向干扰】：7段①句提到尽管机器人医生和外科医生可能相差不远，但机器人护士不会决定治疗过程或作出诊断。由此可知，医生和外科医生并不会因为机器人而很快下岗，可以排除A）“医生和外科医生很快就会下岗”。

B选项【无中生有】：原文并未提及机器人行业的发展前景，可以排除B）“机器人行业不久之后就会腾飞”。

D选项【偷换概念】：7段③句提到的是机器人的融人将带来合作而非替代，并未提及合作不会取代竞争，可以排除D）“合作不会取代竞争”
